categories.title: Brand Guidelines
categories.description: The rulebook for your brand. Clear rules for logo, colour and type, so every future design stays on point.
categories.outcome: Everything anyone needs to use your brand without asking you first.
categories.intro: A logo is one asset. A brand is a system — and the moment a second person touches it (a printer, a developer, a freelancer, a future employee) the system either holds or drifts. Guidelines are what keep the fifth thing you make look related to the first.
deliverables: Logo system: every version, with clear-space, sizing and misuse rules
Colour palette with HEX, RGB and CMYK values
Typography: typefaces, weights, hierarchy and usage
Layout, grid and composition principles
Imagery, texture and graphic-element direction
Do / don't pages so misuse is obvious
Delivered as a presentation-ready PDF
goodFor: Brands about to hand work to other designers, printers or agencies
Businesses that have outgrown a single logo file
Founders who want the brand to stay consistent as the team grows

categories.title: Logo Design
categories.description: Marks that stick. Every logo ships in SVG, PDF and PNG with color and mono versions.
categories.outcome: A mark that holds up at 16 pixels and on a shopfront.
categories.intro: Most logos fail somewhere: they blur at favicon size, fall apart in one colour, or look like three other businesses in the same category. The work starts from what your brand actually has to survive — a phone screen, an embroidered shirt, a printed invoice — and designs backwards from that.
deliverables: Primary logo, plus a stacked or horizontal lockup where the layout needs one
Full-colour, single-colour and reversed (light-on-dark) versions
Vector source files: SVG, PDF and AI
Transparent PNGs at web and print resolution
Favicon / app-icon crop
Clear-space and minimum-size rules
goodFor: New businesses naming and launching for the first time
Established businesses whose mark no longer matches the work
Founders who need one asset that works everywhere, today

categories.title: Logo Animation
categories.description: Logo reveals and motion identities in MP4 and GIF, ready for web, decks and social.
categories.intro: A static mark says what you are. A mark that resolves in motion says you built something. Animation is the smallest upgrade with the largest perceived one — it is the first frame of a video, the loader on a site, the sting at the end of an ad.
deliverables: Logo reveal / intro animation
MP4 for web, decks and video
GIF for email and messaging
Transparent version where the format allows
Sized for the placements you name
goodFor: Brands producing video, ads or pitch decks
Sites and apps that need a branded loading moment
Anyone whose identity already exists and needs one more dimension

categories.title: Social Media Kit
categories.description: Feed templates, stories and campaign tiles sized for every platform and built to stop the scroll.
categories.outcome: A feed that looks designed rather than assembled.
categories.intro: Social is where most brands quietly come apart — a different font every week, a logo squashed into a circle, screenshots posted as artwork. The fix is not more posts, it is a small set of templates that are faster to use than to ignore.
deliverables: Feed post templates covering your recurring post types
Story and reel-cover templates
Profile picture and cover art, cropped per platform
Highlight covers
Editable source files so you can publish without a designer
goodFor: Brands posting regularly with no visual system
Founders who publish their own content and want it to look consistent
Launches that need a coherent campaign set

categories.title: Stationery Design
categories.description: Business cards, letterheads and envelopes, print ready for any shop.
categories.outcome: Print files you can send to any printer without a phone call.
categories.intro: Stationery is where a brand stops being a screen and becomes an object someone holds. It is also where amateur work shows fastest — wrong bleed, low-resolution logos, type that dies at the trim. Files go out print-ready, with bleed and crop marks, so the print shop has nothing to query.
deliverables: Business card, front and back
Letterhead sized for A4 and US Letter
Envelope (DL / #10)
Email signature
Print-ready PDFs with bleed and crop marks
Editable source files
goodFor: Brands going to print for the first time
Studios, clinics and practices that hand over cards in person
Anyone whose current stationery was made in a word processor
